title: Fake US thinktank set up and funded by Israel sought to game AI for propaganda

reading.body:
The Hanover Institute incident is an example of a content pipeline built specifically to manipulate AI retrieval rather than to inform human readers directly. The operation published more than 560,000 words across 124 reports in nine days, with headlines formatted as questions users would type into chatbots, and the platform itself was designed to optimize content for AI systems. The goal was to cause chatbots to surface pro-Israel arguments on contested topics, presented as neutral research, when users queried those subjects.

The failure this exposes sits inside the training and retrieval pipelines of AI systems, not in any single model response. When large volumes of professionally formatted, seemingly sourced content flood the web, systems that ingest or retrieve that content have no reliable mechanism to detect coordinated inauthenticity at ingestion time. A human editorial check on sources would not catch this automatically either, because the institute mimicked the surface conventions of a legitimate think tank, including report formatting and neutral-sounding framing, while having no physical address, no named staff, and no legal existence.

What is not established is whether any specific AI system's outputs were measurably altered by this content, or whether the broader campaign achieved its stated goals. The filing with the US Justice Department classifies the material as foreign propaganda, but that registration is not a legal finding of wrongdoing. The reported frustration among Israeli officials and the polling decline in American sympathy are presented as related context, but a causal link between the AI-targeting campaign and those figures is not demonstrated in the reporting.

reports.title: Fake US thinktank set up and funded by Israel sought to game AI for propaganda

summary:
# Summary

An Israeli-funded fake American think tank called the Hanover Institute published over 560,000 words across 124 reports in nine days using a platform designed to optimize content for AI chatbots. The website presents pro-Israel arguments on topics including Palestinian torture, Israeli war crimes, and Gaza starvation as neutral research, with all headlines formatted as questions users might ask chatbots. The New York production company Piro Inc filed the operation with the US Justice Department as Israeli government propaganda material. The institute claims no legal existence, has no physical address or named staff, and initially denied external funding before later contradicting that statement.

The campaign is part of a broader Israeli government effort, financed by tens of millions of dollars through the European advertising group Havas Media, aimed at influencing artificial intelligence systems to promote Israel's position. Israeli officials have privately expressed frustration that the expensive public diplomacy campaign has failed, with American support for Israel significantly declining. Recent polling shows 36 percent of Americans sympathize with Israel, down from higher levels, and 60 percent view Israel unfavorably as of April 2026.
